newsitem.title: UK: UK GDP adds fuel to BOE's call for higher rates.
newsitem.headline: UK GDP adds fuel to BOE's call for higher rates.

text.p: An upward revision to second quarter UK GDP brings economic growth perilously close to the trend rate and will lead to louder calls for a rise in interest rates, left on hold for the next month at 5.75 percent.
GDP was revised up to 2.2 percent from 1.8 percent at the last estimate. Trend growth is estimated at around 2.4 percent.

"GDP has not been that soft to begin with this year and anecdotal and survey evidence suggests it will accelerate as the year unfolds, so monetary policy is clearly too loose," said Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.
The Bank of England has upped the ante at recent monetary meetings when Governor Eddie George said he would prefer to see rates back up at 6.0 percent.
Economists said George undoubtedly made the same request at Monday's monetary meeting, but Clarke rejected the advice. This is likely to be the shape of monetary meetings in the months ahead.
"The debate will now clearly shift from possible rate cuts to whether the government can resist pressure for a rate rise before the general election," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.
Stewart said Clarke may be forced to rise above the political difficulties and raise the cost of borrowing as the outlook for future inflation deteriorates ahead of the election.
"Growth in the months ahead will show spare capacity is being eliminated and the labour market tightening further, and you can't reconcile that with a 2.5 percent inflation target."
A breakdown of the final GDP figures showed output from construction and a broad range of service industries grew much faster than previously thought.

Gardiner said the upward revision to service industry output was expected. "We thought there was a bit more happening in the economy than the first estimates showed. When inventories are stripped out growth is now well above trend."
The slower rate of stock building in the second quarter knocked 0.9 percent off GDP, so adjusted for inventories GDP grew 1.4 percent on the quarter.

Gardiner agreed a pre-election rate rise should not be ruled out. "Clarke has so much political capital invested in being a sensible Chancellor and it could backfire if he is perceived to be bribing the electorate with tax cuts and lower rates."
"I think he'll bite the bullet and raise rates by February, before the election campaign gets into full swing," said Gardiner. A general election must be held by May 1997.

Second quarter current account data, also released on Tuesday, showed a surprise surplus of 457 million sterling, the largest surplus since the first quarter in 1987. This compares with a deficit in Q1 revised down to 786 million stg.
"These are spectacularly good numbers," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "The improvement came entirely from the non-goods side. Investment income in particular has risen sharply."

Earnings from services also rebounded, helped by activity related to Britain hosting the Euro 96 Football Championships. "That added between 100 and 200 million stg exports of services in the quarter," Loynes said.
The improvement in the trade picture will help allay fears that the pick-up in economic activity, and consumer spending in particular, will result in a worsening of the balance of payments.
